articles.description: Before ordering a small batch, build one complete unit: check how the board fits, where the cable goes, how it assembles and opens, and what the next build is for.

The original WIZnet board tutorial introduces processor power using the annotated pin reference below. It helps separate the supply for digital I/O from the supply for the chip's core and the input to its regulator.
RP2350 power pins fall into separate groups: IOVDD supplies the digital I/O, DVDD supplies the chip's digital core, and VREG_VIN is the input to its on-chip regulator.
The tutorial's accompanying description of two independent core LDOs does not match that design and should not be used as wiring instructions.
These are proposed migration checks; the source tutorial does not document this experiment.

The values match [RP2040 datasheet Table 622](https://datasheets.raspberrypi.com/rp2040/rp2040-datasheet.pdf). The tutorial places them under an EVB-Pico2 heading, so do not assume they specify an RP2350-based board. Check the fitted chip, pin type and current datasheet.

Pin voltage limits, such as those in [RP2040 datasheet Table 622](https://datasheets.raspberrypi.com/rp2040/rp2040-datasheet.pdf), are expressed relative to the I/O supply. When a receiving supply changes, a signal that was acceptable during normal operation may no longer be acceptable. Check the fitted chip, pin type and current datasheet.

The MAC section of FreakStudio's WIZnet MicroPython tutorial provides the useful starting point: an Ethernet frame carries separate source and destination addresses. Its diagrams explain the format; they do not demonstrate provisioning or testing a batch of devices. Here we use that reference to plan the step from one working prototype to several distinguishable units.
